source_text: De octo spiritibus malitiae (sub nomine Nili Ancyrani) ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΩΝ ΟΚΤΩ ΠΝΕΥΜΑΤΩΝ ΤΗΣ ΠΟΝΗΡΙΑΣ. ΚΕΦΑΛ. Λʹ. Περὶ γαστριμαργίας. Ἀρχὴ καρποφορίας, ἄνθος, καὶ ἀρχὴ πρακτικῆς, ἐγκράτεια· ὁ κρατῶν γαστρὸς, ἐλαττοῖ πάθη, ἡττώμενος δὲ βρώμασιν αὔξει τὰς ἡδονάς. Ἀρχὴ ἐθνῶν Ἀμαλὴκ, καὶ ἀρχὴ παθῶν γαστριμαργία. Ὕλη πυρὸς ξύλα, ὕλη δὲ γαστρὸς βρώματα. Ξύλα πολλὰ μεγάλην ἐγείρει φλόγα, πλῆθος δὲ βρωμάτων τρέφει ἐπιθυμίαν. Φλὸξ ἀμαυροῦται ἐπιλειπούσης ὕλης, καὶ βρωμάτων ἔνδεια μαραίνει ἐπιθυμίαν. Ὁ κρατήσας σιαγόνος, ἀνεῖλεν ἀλλοφύλους, καὶ δεσμὰ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ διέσπασεν εὐχερῶς. Ἀναίρεσις σιαγόνος πηγὴν ἐγέννησεν ὕδατος, καὶ γαστριμαργία καταργηθεῖσα, θεωρίαν ἔτεκε πρακτικήν. Πάσσαλος σκηνῆς παρελθὼν, σιαγόνα ἀνεῖλε πολέμιον, καὶ λόγος ἐγκρατείας ἐνέκρωσε πάθος. Ἐπιθυμία βρώσεως ἔτεκε παρακοὴν, καὶ γεῦσις ἡδεῖα ἐξέβαλε παραδείσου. Πολυτέλεια βρωμάτων τέρπει λαιμὸν, τρέφει δὲ σκώληκα ἀκολασίας ἀκοίμητον. Ἐνδεὴς γαστὴρ ἐν προσευχῇ ἀγρυπνεῖν παρασκευάζει, ἡ δὲ πεπληρωμένη ὕπνον ἐπάγει πολύν. Νηφάλιον φρόνημα ἐν ξηροτάτῃ διαίτῃ, ὑγρὸς δὲ βίος βαπτίζει νοῦν εἰς βυθόν. Νηστεύοντος προσευχὴ, νεοσσὸς ἀετοῦ ἀνιπτάμενος, ἡ δὲ τοῦ κραιπαλοῦντος βαρυνομένη τῷ κόρῳ, καθέλκεται· νηστεύοντος νοῦς, ἀστὴρ ἐν αἰθρίᾳ λαμπρὸς, ὁ δὲ τοῦ κραιπαλοῦντος ἐν σκοτομήνῃ καλύπτεται· ὀμίχλη καλύπτει ἡλιακὰς ἀκτῖνας, καὶ νοῦν σκοτίζει παχεῖα βρωμάτων ἀνάδοσις. ΚΕΦΑΛ. Βʹ. Ἔσοπτρον ῥυπωθὲν οὐ διαρθροῖ τὴν προσπεσοῦσαν μορφὴν, καὶ διανοητικὸν ἀμβλυνθὲν κόρῳ, οὐ δέχεται γνῶσιν Θεοῦ. Χερσωθεῖσα γῆ ἀκάνθας τίκτει, καὶ νοῦς γαστριμάργου βλαστάνει λογισμοὺς αἰσχρούς. Οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν βορβόρῳ εὑρεῖν ἀρώματα, οὐδὲ ἐν γαστριμάργῳ θεωρίας εὐωδίαν. Ὀφθαλμὸς γαστριμάργου περιεργάζεται συμπόσια· ὀφθαλμὸς δὲ ἐγκρατοῦς συνέδρια σοφῶν. Μνήμας μαρτύρων ἀριθμεῖ ψυχὴ γαστριμάργου, ἡ δὲ τοῦ ἐγκρατοῦς μιμεῖται βίους αὐτῶν. ∆ειλὸς στρατιώτης φρίσσει σάλπιγγα σημαίνουσαν πόλεμον, καὶ γαστρίμαργος κηρυσσομένην ἐγκράτειαν. Γαστρίμαργος μοναχὸς, κοιλίας ὑπόφορος, καὶ μαστιζόμενος ἀπαιτεῖται δα79.1148 σμὸν ἡμερούσιον. Ὁδοιπόρος ὀξὺς ταχέως καταλήψεται πόλιν, καὶ μοναχὸς ἐγκρατὴς εἰρηνικὴν κατάστασιν· ὁδοιπόρος βραδὺς ἐν ἐρημίᾳ αὐλισθήσεται ὕπαιθρος, καὶ μοναχὸς γαστρίμαργος οὐ φθάσει εἰς οἶκον ἀπαθείας. Ἀτμὶς θυμιάματος εὐωδιάζει ἀέρα, καὶ προσευχὴ ἐγκρατοῦς ὄσφρησιν Θεοῦ. Ἐὰν δῷς σεαυτὸν ἐπιθυμίᾳ βρωμάτων, οὐδὲν ἀρκέσει πρὸς τὸ πληρῶσαι τὴν ἡδονήν· πῦρ γάρ ἐστιν ἐπιθυμία βρωμάτων, ἀεὶ δεχομένη, καὶ ἀεὶ φλεγομένη. Μέτρον αὔταρκες ἐπλήρωσεν ἀγγεῖον, γαστὴρ δὲ ῥηγνυμένη, οὐ λέγει, Ἀρκεῖ. Χειρῶν ἔκτασις ἐτροπώσατο τὸν Ἀμαλὴκ, καὶ πράξεις ἐπηρμέναι χειροῦνται πάθη σαρκός. ΚΕΦΑΛ. Γʹ. Ἐξολόθρευσον ἐκ σοῦ πᾶν ἔμπνεον κακίας, καὶ μέλη σαρκός σου νέκρωσον ἰσχυρῶς. Ὃν τρόπον γὰρ ἀνῃρημένος πολέμιος, οὐ παρέξει σοι φόβον, οὕτω νεκρωθὲν σῶμα οὐ ταράξει σου τὴν ψυχήν. Οὐκ οἶδε πυρὸς ὀδύνην σῶμα νεκρὸν, οὐδὲ ἐγκρατὴς ἡδονὴν ἐπιθυμίας νεκρᾶς. Ἐὰν πατάξῃς Αἰγύπτιον, ἐν ἄμμῳ κρύψον αὐτὸν, καὶ μὴ πιάνῃς σῶμα ἐπὶ ἡττωμένῳ πάθει· ὡς γὰρ ἐν λιπώσῃ γῇ φύει 1 τὸ κρυφθὲν, οὕτως ἐν σώματι πιμελώδει ἀναθάλλει τὸ πάθος. Μαρανθεῖσα φλὸξ ἀναλάμπει ἐπιλαβομένη φρυγάνων, καὶ ἡδονὴ σβεσθεῖσα ἀναζωπυροῦται ἐν κόρῳ βρωμάτων. Μὴ ἐλεήσῃς σῶμα ἀτονίαν ἀποδυρόμενον, μηδὲ πιάνῃς αὐτὸ πολυτελείᾳ βρωμάτων· ἐὰν γὰρ ἰσχύσῃ, ἐπαναστήσεταί σοι, καὶ πόλεμον ἄσπονδον κινήσει κατὰ σοῦ, ἕως ἂν αἰχμαλωτεύσῃ σὴν ψυχὴν, καὶ δοῦλον παραδώσει σε τῷ τῆς πορνείας πάθει. Ἵππος εὐήνιος, ἐνδεὲς σῶμα, καὶ οὐ μὴ καταβαλεῖ τὸν ἀναβάτην ποτὲ, ὁ μὲν γὰρ εἴκει ἀγχόμενος χαλινῷ, καὶ τῇ χειρὶ πείθεται τοῦ ἡνιόχου, σῶμα δὲ δαμάζεται ἐν λιμῷ, καὶ ἀγρυπνίᾳ, καὶ οὐκ ἀποσκιρτᾷ τοῦ ἐπιβατοῦντος λογισμοῦ, οὐδὲ
english: On the eight spirits of malice (under the name of Nilus of Ancyra). The same, concerning the eight spirits of malice. Chapter 4. Concerning gluttony. The beginning of fruitfulness is the flower, and the beginning of practice is self-control; he who masters the stomach diminishes passions, but he who is defeated by foods increases pleasures. The beginning of the Amalekite nation is the source of passions, and the beginning of passions is gluttony. The matter of fire is wood, and the matter of the stomach is foods. Many woods raise a great flame, and a multitude of foods nourishes desire. The flame is extinguished when the matter remains, and the desire withers when the food is scarce. He who seized the bit drove out the foreigners, and the bonds of his hands he easily broke apart. The removal of the bit produced a spring of water, and gluttony having been abolished, it gave birth to practical contemplation. Having passed through the Passover of the tent (Exodus 12), he removed the bit of the enemy, and the word of self-control suppressed the passion. The desire for eating gave birth to disobedience, and a sweet taste cast out [one] from paradise (Genesis 3). The abundance of foods delights the throat, but nourishes the sleepless worms of intemperance. A hungry stomach prepares one to keep watch in prayer, but a full one brings on much sleep. Sobriety of mind is found in a very dry diet, but a moist life immerses the intellect into a depth. For one fasting, prayer is like an eagle's fledgling rising up, but the one weighed down by the heaviness of the neck is dragged down; for one fasting, the mind is a bright star in the clear sky, but the one weighed down is covered in darkness; as mist covers the solar rays, so the thick exhalation of foods darkens the intellect. Chapter 2. A mirror having become soiled does not shatter the form approaching it, and the intellect having been dulled by heaviness does not receive the knowledge of God. A parched land brings forth thorns, and the mind of a glutton sprouts shameful thoughts. It is not possible to find fragrances in a mire, nor in a glutton the sweetness of contemplation. The eye of a glutton searches out banquets; but the eye of the self-controlled [searches out] the assemblies of the wise. The soul of a glutton counts the memories of martyrs, but the [soul] of the self-controlled...

He mimics their lives. A cowardly soldier shudders at a trumpet signaling war, and a glutton at the proclamation of self-control. A gluttonous monk, a subverter of the belly, is required to undergo a daily fast.

A traveler quickly reaches a city, and a self-controlled monk, a peaceful state; a slow traveler will stumble in the wilderness, exposed, and a gluttonous monk will not reach the house of apatheia. A wisp of incense sweetens the air, and the prayer of one self-controlled, the scent of God. If you give yourself to the desire of foods, nothing will suffice to fulfill the pleasure; for the desire of foods is a fire, always receiving and always burning. A sufficient measure filled a vessel, but a bursting stomach does not say, 'It is enough.' The stretching out of hands turned the Amalekite (Exodus 17:12), and sinful actions are the result of the passions of the flesh.

Chapter 4. Destroy from yourself every breath of evil, and kill the members of your flesh strongly. For in the same way that a defeated enemy will not present fear to you, so a dead body will not disturb your soul. A dead body knows not the pain of fire, nor does a self-controlled person the pleasure of a dead desire. If you strike an Egyptian, hide him in the sand, and do not take up a body upon a defeated passion; for just as that which is hidden grows in a deserted land, so the passion sprouts up in a greasy body. A withered flame relights itself by taking up embers, and a pleasure having been extinguished is rekindled in the heap of foods. Do not show mercy to a body losing its strength, nor take it up with the luxury of foods; for if it is strong, it will rise up against you, and it will stir up unceasing war against you, until it captures your soul and delivers you as a slave to the passion of fornication.

A well-trained horse, being within the body, will never cast down the rider; for indeed it goes constrained by the bit, and obeys the hand of the driver, but the body is tamed by fasting and wakefulness, and it does not depart from the thought of the one riding upon it, nor...

source_text: χρεμετίσει κινούμενον ὑπὸ ὁρμῆς ἐμπαθοῦς. ΚΕΦΑΛ. ∆ʹ. Περὶ πορνείας. Σωφροσύνην τίκτει ἐγκράτεια, γαστριμαργία δὲ, μήτηρ ἀκολασίας· ἔλαιον τρέφει λαμπάδα λύχνου, καὶ πυρσὸν ἡδονῆς ἐξάπτει συντυχία γυναικῶν. Κυμάτων βία χειμάζει πλοῖον ἀνερμάτιστον, καὶ λογισμὸς πορνείας, νοῦν ἀκρατῆ. Πορνεία συμπαραλήψεται κόρον εἰς συμμαχίαν, ἀφήσει γὰρ αὐτὸν, καὶ μετὰ τῶν ἐναντίων στήσεται, καὶ ἐπ' ἐσχάτων συμπολεμήσει τοῖς ἐχθροῖς. Ἄτρωτος διαμένει ἀπὸ τῶν βελῶν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ ὁ ἀγαπῶν ἡσυχίαν, συναναμιγνύμενος δὲ πλήθει συνεχεῖς δέχεται πληγάς. Ὄψις γυναικὸς βέλος ἐστὶ πεφαρμακευμένον, ἔτρωσε τὴν ψυχὴν, καὶ τὸν ἰὸν ἐναπέθετο, καὶ ὅσον χρονίζει, πλείονα τὴν σῆψιν ἐργάζεται. Ὁ φυλασσόμενος 79.1149 ταῦτα τὰ βέλη, οὐ παραβάλλει πανηγύρεσι πανδήμοις, οὐδὲ ἐν ταῖς ἑορταῖς περιάξει κεχηνώς· βέλτιον γὰρ οἴκοι μένοντα σχολάζειν προσευχαῖς, ἢ τιμᾷν νομίζοντα τὰς ἑορτὰς, γίνεσθαι πάρεργον ἐχθρῶν. Φεῦγε συντυχίαν γυναικῶν, ἐὰν θέλῃς σωφρονεῖν, καὶ μὴ δῷς παῤῥησίαν αὐταῖς θαῤῥῆσαί σοί ποτε. Εὐλάβειαν γὰρ ἐν ἀρχαῖς ἢ ἔχουσιν ἢ ὑποκρίνονται· ὕστερον δὲ πάντα τολμῶσιν ἀναιδῶς· πρώτῃ συντυχίᾳ τὸ βλέμμα ἔχουσι κάτω, λαλοῦσι πράως, καὶ δακρύουσι συμπαθῶς, σχηματίζονται σεμνῶς, καὶ στενάζουσι πικρὰ, ἐρωτῶσι περὶ ἁγνείας, καὶ ἀκούουσι σπουδαίως· δεύτερον εἶδες, καὶ μικρὸν ἀνένευσαν ἄνω· τρίτον, καὶ προσέχουσιν ἀναιδῶς, ἐμειδιάσας, κἀκεῖναι κεχυμένως ἐγέλασαν· κοσμοῦνται λοιπὸν, καὶ ἐνδείκνυνταί σοι σαφῶς, βλέμμα μορφοῦσιν εὐαγγελιζόμεναι τὸ πάθος, ὀφρῦς ἀνατείνουσι, καὶ περιστρέφουσι βλέφαρα, γυμνοῦσι τὸν τράχηλον, καὶ ὅλῳ τῷ σώματι θρύπτονται, λόγους λαλοῦσι μαλάσσοντας τὸ πάθος, καὶ φθέγμα ἐπιτηδεύουσι θέλγηστρον ἀκοῆς, ἕως ἂν διὰ πάντων πολιορκήσωσι τὴν ψυχήν. Ταῦτα γίνεταί σοι ἄγκιστρα δελεάζοντα εἰς θάνατον, καὶ θήρατρα πολύπλοκα ἕλκοντα εἰς ἀπώλειαν, μή σε πλανήσωσι λόγοις ἐπιεικῶς κεχρημέναι· ἐγκέκρυπται γὰρ αὐταῖς ἰὸς πονηρὸς θηρίων. ΚΕΦΑΛ. Εʹ. Μᾶλλον προσέγγισον πυρὶ καιομένῳ, ἢ γυναικὶ νέᾳ, νέος ὢν καὶ αὐτός· πυρὶ μὲν γὰρ προσελθὼν, καὶ ὀδυνηθεὶς, ταχέως ἀποπηδήσεις, γυναικείοις δὲ ῥήμασι χαυνωθεὶς, οὐκ εὐχερῶς ἀναχωρήσεις. Θάλλει βοτάνη ἑστῶσα παρ' ὕδατι, καὶ πάθος ἀκολασίας ἐν συντυχίᾳ γυναικῶν. Ὁ πληρῶν γαστέρα, καὶ ἐπαγγελλόμενος σωφρονεῖν, ὅμοιός ἐστι τῷ λέγοντι, χαλινοῦν πυρὸς ἐνέργειαν ἐν καλάμῃ. Ὃν τρόπον γὰρ πυρὸς ῥοπὴν ἐν καλάμῃ τρέχουσαν ἀδύνατον ἐπισχεῖν, οὕτως ὁρμὴν ἀκόλαστον φλεγομένην ἐν κόρῳ παῦσαι ἀδύνατον. Στύλος ἐπερείδεται βάσει, καὶ πορνείας πάθος ἐπαναπαύεται κόρῳ. Εἰς λιμένα ἐπείγεται χειμαζομένη ναῦς, καὶ ψυχὴ σώφρονος ἐπιζητεῖ ἐρημίαν· φεύγει ἡ μὲν κύματα θαλάσσης ἀπειλοῦντα κίνδυνον, ἡ δὲ μορφὰς γυναικῶν ὀδυνούσας ὄλεθρον. Μορφὴ κεκαλλωπισμένη κύματος χεῖρον βυθίζει· τοῦ μὲν γὰρ ἕστι καὶ διανήξασθαι, πόθῳ ζωῆς, μορφὴ δὲ γυναικὸς ἀπατήσασα, καταφρονεῖν πείθει καὶ αὐτῆς τῆς ζωῆς. Βάτος ἐρημικὴ διαφεύγει φλόγα πυρὸς ἀβλαβῶς, καὶ σώφρων κεχωρισμένος γυναικῶν οὐκ 2 ἐφλογίσθη ἀκολασίας πάθει· ὥσπερ γὰρ μνήμη πυρὸς οὐ καίει διάνοιαν, οὕτω οὐδὲ πάθος ἰσχύει, μὴ παρούσης ὕλης. ΚΕΦΑΛ. ϛʹ. Ἐὰν ἐλεήσῃς πολέμιον, ἕσται σοι ἐχθρὸς, καὶ ἐὰν φείσῃ πάθους, ἐπαναστήσεταί σοι. Ἀκόλαστον ἐρεθίζει πρὸς ἠδονὴν ὅψις γυναικὸς, τὸν δὲ σώφρονα κανεῖ 79.1152 πρὸς δοξολογίαν Θεοῦ· ἐὰν ἠρεμήσῃ τὸ πάθος ἐν συντυχίαις γυναικῶν, μὴ πιστεύσῃς αὐτῷ ἀπάθειαν ἐπαγγελλομένῳ. Καὶ γὰρ κύων σαίνει μὲν ἀπολειφθεὶς ὄχλῳ, ἔξω δὲ προελθὼν, τὴν οἰκείαν ἐπιδείκνυται πονηρίαν. Ὅταν γυναικὸς μνήμη γένηται ἀπαθῶς, τότε νόμιζε τῶν ὅρων ἐπιβεβηκέναι τῆς σωφροσύνης. Ὅτε δέ σε τὸ εἴδωλον αὐτῆς ἐπὶ θεωρίαν διεγείρει, καὶ τὰ βέλη αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχήν σου περιλαμβάνουσι, τότε νόμιζε ἔξω εἶναι τῆς ἀρετῆς. Ἀλλὰ μηδὲ οὕτως ἐγχρονίσῃς τοῖς τοιούτοις λογισμοῖς, μηδὲ ἐπὶ πολὺ κατὰ διάνοιαν προσομιλήσῃς μορφῇ γυναικὸς, ἔστι γὰρ φιλυπόστροφον τὸ πάθος, καὶ τὸν κίνδυνον ἔχει ἐγγύς. Ὥσπερ γὰρ ἡ σύμμετρος χωνεία καθαίρει τὸν ἄργυρον, ἡ δὲ ἐπὶ πολὺ καὶ ἀπόλλυσιν εὐχερῶς, οὕτως ἕξιν σωφρονικὴν διαφθείρει ἐγχρονίζουσα φαντασία γυναικός· μηδὲ ἐπὶ πολὺ προσομιλήσῃς τῷ φανέντι προσώπῳ, ἵνα μὴ ἀνάψῃ ἐν σοὶ ἡδονῆς φλόγα, καὶ ἐμπρήσῃ ἅλωνα σῆς ψυχῆς· ὥσπερ γὰρ σπινθὴρ ἐν ἀχύροις χρονίσας ἐγείρει φλόγα, οὕτω μνήμη γυναικὸς παραμένουσα ἐξάπτει ἐπιθυμίαν. ΚΕΦΑΛ. Ζʹ. Περὶ φιλαργυρίας. Φιλαργυρία πάντων ἐστὶ ῥίζα τῶν κακῶν, καὶ τρέφει ὡς κλάδους πονηροὺς τὰ λοιπὰ πάθη, καὶ οὐκ ἀφήσει ξηρανθῆναι τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς
english: [It will be] moved by a passionate impulse.

Chapter 4. On Fornication. Temperance gives birth to self-control, but gluttony is the mother of licentiousness; oil feeds the flame of a lamp, and the company of women kindles a torch of pleasure. The violence of waves wrecks an unmoored ship, and the thought of fornication [destroys] an uncontrolled mind. Fornication will take a youth as an ally, for it will leave him and stand with the adversaries, and in the end, it will fight alongside the enemies. He who loves stillness remains unharmed from the arrows of the enemy, but he who mixes himself with the crowd receives continuous wounds.

The sight of a woman is a poisoned arrow; it wounded the soul and deposited its venom, and as long as it lingers, it works more rot. He who guards himself against these arrows does not compare them to public festivals, nor does he surround himself with them during feasts; for it is better to remain at home idling in prayers, than to become a tool for enemies while thinking one honors the feasts. Flee the company of women, if you wish to be temperate, and do not give them boldness, lest they ever tear you apart. For they have piety in the beginning, either truly or pretending; but later they dare everything shamelessly.

At the first meeting, they cast their eyes down, speak softly, and weep sympathetically; they fashion themselves solemnly and sigh bitterly; they ask about purity and listen earnestly. Second, I saw, and they slightly lifted [their eyes] upward; third, they pay attention shamelessly, having smiled, and they laughed when [you] were poured out; thereafter they adorn themselves, and clearly show you, shaping their gaze, being delighted by the passion, they raise their eyebrows and roll their eyelids, they expose the neck, and they agitate themselves with their whole body; they speak words softening the passion, and use a tone that is an enticement to the ear, until through all these things they besiege the soul. These things become hooks to lure you toward death, and complex snares to drag you toward destruction, lest they mislead you with words used quite decently; for a wicked venom of beasts is hidden within them.

Chapter 5. Rather approach a burning fire than a young woman, being a young man yourself; for approaching fire, though pained, you will quickly leap away, but being softened by feminine words, you will not easily withdraw. Vegetation flourishes standing by water, and a passion of licentiousness in company...

One who is full of belly and promises to be temperate is like one who tries to restrain the energy of fire in a reed. For just as it is impossible to stop a stream of fire running in a reed, it is impossible to stop an uncontrolled, burning impulse in the genitals. A pillar relies on its base, and the passion of fornication rests in the genitals. A ship tossed by storms hastens to a harbor, and a temperate soul seeks solitude; the former flees the waves of the sea threatening danger, while the latter flees the form of women mourning destruction. A form adorned like a wave sinks the hand deeper; for the one is able to pass through by the desire for life, but the form of a woman, having deceived, persuades one to despise even life itself. The desert bush avoids the flame of fire without harm, and the temperate one, having separated from women, was not ignited by the passion of incontinence; for just as the memory of fire does not burn the intellect, so also passion has no power when the material is not present.

Chapter 6. If you show mercy to an enemy, he will be an enemy to you, and if you spare the passion, it will rise up against you. The sight of a woman stirs up uncontrolled impulse toward pleasure, but it makes the temperate man turn toward the glorification of God; if the passion becomes calm in the company of women, do not believe in its promised apathy. For even a dog barks when left with a crowd, but having come out, it shows its domestic wickedness. When the memory of a woman arises apathetically, then consider that the boundaries of temperance have been established. But when the idol of her arises for contemplation, and her arrows surround your soul, then consider that you are outside of virtue. But do not even thus entertain such thoughts, nor for long converse in the intellect with the form of a woman, for the passion is turn-loving, and the danger is near. Just as a well-proportioned crucible purifies silver, but one that is [poorly made] for long [use] easily destroys it, so a fantasy of a woman destroys temperance by entertaining it; do not converse for long with the appearing face, so that the flame of pleasure may not ignite in you and surround the net of your soul; for just as a spark, having stayed in unlit places, raises a flame, so a remaining memory of a woman inflames desire.
Chapter 7. Concerning avarice. Avarice is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10), and it feeds the remaining passions like evil branches, and it will not let those things from it be dried up.

A greedy monk is like a heavily laden ship, easily diving into the surge of waves; for just as a ship overloaded by each wave is tormented, so the greedy one becomes submerged by his cares. An ungreedy monk is a steady traveler, finding lodging in every place. An ungreedy monk is a high-flying eagle, descending to food only when necessity compels him.

Such a person is higher than every temptation; he scoffs at what is present and is lifted up, suspended in the air, withdrawing from earthly things and making his life among the higher things; for he has a light wing, not weighed down by cares. If tribulation comes, he leaves the place without being crushed; if death approaches, he departs straightway; for he has not bound his soul to any earthly thing.

But the greedy one is prostrate with anxieties, and just as a dog is bound in a chain, even if he is forced to repent, he circles the memories of his possessions like a heavy and useless burden; he is stung by grief, and toward the thought of them he suffers intensely; he has left the possessions, yet he is scourged by the grief of them. Even if death comes, he pitifully lets go of what is present and gives up his soul, yet his eye does not depart from things; his limb is pulled away like a runaway slave, divided from the body, but not divided from things, rather being held by the passion that pulls him.

The sea is not filled even though it receives a multitude of rivers, and the desire for silver is not satisfied by things; he has doubled his money, and he desires to make these things double as well, and he never ceases doubling, until death stops this unceasing haste.

A prudent monk will attend to the body's needs, and will fill the stomach's need with bread and water; he will not flatter the wealthy for the pleasure of the stomach, nor will he enslave a free mind to many masters; for the hands are sufficient to serve the body and to fulfill natural necessity in all things. An ungreedy monk is an unhesitating athlete and a light runner, quickly reaching the prize of the higher calling. A greedy monk rejoices in many arrivals, but the ungreedy...

Those who have achieved [virtue] are crowned. A silver-loving monk works hard, but the generous man occupies himself with prayers and readings. A silver-loving monk fills treasuries of gold, but the generous man stores up in heaven. 'Accursed is he who makes an idol and places it in secret' (Exodus 20:4), just so is he who has the passion of silver-loving; for the one worships a deceptive, unprofitable thing, but the other carries the phantom of wealth.

CHAPTER 8. Concerning Anger. Anger is a manic passion, and it easily deranges those who have knowledge, making the soul beast-like and making every encounter a turning away. A violent wind will not move a tower, and a wrathless spirit is not seized by fury. Water is moved by the force of winds, and the wrathful man is tossed by irrational thoughts. A monk in anger saw something and gnashed his teeth. A rising mist thickens the air, and a movement of fury thickens the intellect of the angry man. A cloud running before darkened the sun, and a thought of grudge darkens the mind. A lion being in a painting constantly moves the feathers, and the wrathful man in a cell [moves] thoughts of anger. Pleasant is contemplation, a calm sea, but there is nothing more pleasant than a peaceful state; for in a calm sea dolphins swim, but in a peaceful state, God-befitting thoughts are immersed. A long-suffering monk is a quieting spring, providing a gentle drink to all, but the intellect of the angry man is scattered through all things and will not give water to the thirsty; and even if he gives, it is muddied and useless, and the eyes of the wrathful are disordered, and they are mists and angels of the troubled heart. But the face of the long-suffering man is set upright, and his eyes are gentle, looking downward.

english: Malice is a sickness of the mind during the time of prayer. The thoughts of the angry are offspring of vipers, and they devour the heart that bore them. The prayer of the angry is a loathsome incense; and the sound of angry psalmody is a dismal noise. The sacrifice of the grudging is an ant-like offering, and it will never approach the altars of the circumcised. The angry man sees disordered dreams, and the wrathful imagines attacks of wild beasts. The patient man sees visions, the meeting of holy angels; and the one who does not hold grudges exercises spiritual discourses, and in the night receives the solutions of mysteries.

Chapter 11. Concerning Sorrow. A monk suffering sorrow does not know spiritual joy; for sorrow is a depression of the soul, and it consists of thoughts of anger. For anger is the defense of desire, and the failure of defense has engendered sorrow; sorrow is the mouth of a lion, and it easily devours the one suffering. Sorrow is a worm of the heart, and it devours the mother who bore it. A mother giving birth to a child, if she has been spared from the pain of labor, does not suffer much; but sorrow being born moves much pain, and remaining after the pangs, she does not suffer a little. A monk suffering sorrow does not know spiritual joy, just as one with a high fever does not taste honey. A monk suffering sorrow will not move the mind toward contemplation, nor will he send up pure prayer; for sorrow is an obstacle to everything good. Fetters of the feet are an obstacle to the race, and sorrow is an obstacle to contemplation. A captive from the barbarians is bound in irons, and a captive from the passions is bound by sorrow. Sorrow is not powerful when other passions are not present, just as a chain is not [powerful] when those binding are not present. He who is bound by sorrow is conquered by the passions, and he brings the bond upon himself as a proof of defeat. For sorrow consists upon the failure of fleshly desire; and desire is joined to every passion. He who conquered desire, conquered the passions; and he who conquered the passions will not be held by sorrow. The self-controlled one is not grieved by the failure of foods, nor the temperate one protesting against unrestrained folly, nor the one without anger falling from defense, nor the humble one being deprived of human honor, nor the one not fond of silver falling into loss; for they strongly diverted that desire; just as one who is armored does not receive an arrow, so the impassive one is not pierced by sorrow.
Chapter 12. A shield to a soldier, and a wall to a city, is security; [and...]

But passion is more dangerous to the monk than both [pleasure and sorrow]; for a whistling arrow has often pierced a gate, and a multitude of soldiers has undermined a wall, but sorrow will not overcome apatheia. He who is mastered by passion has been mastered by sorrow, but he who is defeated by pleasure will not escape its bonds. He who grieves continuously and pretends at apatheia is like one who is sick and pretends at health; for just as the sick man is revealed by his color, so the one full of passion is exposed by sorrow. He who loves the world will be grieved much, but he who holds the things in it in contempt will be joyful through all things. A lover of silver, having been defrauded, will be grieved bitterly, but he who holds things in contempt will be without sorrow. The ambitious man will be grieved when dishonor comes upon him, but the humble-minded man will receive this as a companion. A crucible cleanses unproven silver, and Godly sorrow in sins [is like this]; continuous refining diminishes lead, and worldly sorrow diminishes the intellect. A cloud dims the energy of the eyes, and sorrow blunts the contemplative intellect; a sunbeam does not pass through the depths of water, and the contemplation of light does not shine upon a heavy heart. The rising of the sun is sweet to all men, but even this is displeasing to a grieving soul. The taste of an oyster is taken away from the sense of taste, and sorrow takes away the sense of the soul. But he who holds the pleasures of the world in contempt will not be troubled by thoughts of sorrow.

CHAPTER 13. Concerning Acedia. Acedia is a listlessness of the soul, and a soul lacking listlessness does not stand against trials with courage. For what is nourishment to a healthy body, this is a trial to a courageous soul. The north wind nourishes the crops, and trials confirm the endurance of the soul. A cloud without water is driven by the wind, and the mind lacking endurance is driven by the spirit of acedia. Spring dew increases the fruit of the field, and the spiritual word increases the state of the soul. A flood of acedia drives the monk from his cell, but he who has endurance remains at peace always. When others are weak, the one suffering acedia is cast out, but he who is full of confidence maintains his own purpose. An acedia-stricken monk is sharp toward service, and considers the commandment to be his own confidence; a limp plant was bent by a light breeze, and the fantasy of departure drew the acedia-stricken man away. english: Because it did not bend a soul withdrawn into solitude. A solitary wanderer, a plant of the desert, rests for a little while, and is carried away again, not wishing to stay. A plant being moved about does not bear fruit, and a solitary wanderer will not produce the fruit of virtue. For the weak, a single food is not sufficient, and for the acedia-stricken monk, a single task is not sufficient. For the lover of women, one woman will not suffice, and for the acedia-stricken monk, one cell will not suffice.

Chapter 14. The eye of the acedia-stricken one frequently stares intently at the doors, and his mind imagines those who are visiting; the door has worn down, and he is driven out of himself; he hears a voice, and through the small opening he peers in, and he does not depart from there until he has become numb, sitting there. An acedia-stricken reader experiences many gaps, and is easily carried toward sleep; he rubs his eyes, and stretches out his hands, and having turned his eyes away from the book, he stares intently at the wall, then turning back, he reads a little, and unfolding the ends of the words, he examines them curiously, counts the pages, and calculates the groups of four, scrutinizes the letter and its ornamentation; later, having folded it, he placed the book under his head, and sleeps a sleep not very deep, for hunger subsequently rouses his soul and makes it attend to its own cares. The acedia-stricken monk is sluggish in prayer, and he will never speak the words of prayer; for just as a sick man does not carry a heavy load, so also the acedia-stricken one will never perform the work of God with care; for one is cleansed of the strength of the body, while the other is broken in the tones of the soul. Patience heals acedia, and makes one do all things with much attentiveness and fear of God. Set a measure for yourself in every work, and do not turn away beforehand before you have completed it, and pray sensibly and with speed, and the spirit of acedia will flee from you.

A line drawn through water has become mixed, and the toil of virtue is mixed in a vainglorious soul. A white hand has become covered by the bosom, and a hidden deed of light shines forth more brightly. A briar is entangled in a tree, and...

english: When it reaches the top, it dries up the root, and vainglory clings to virtues and does not depart until it cuts off the power. A cluster of grapes being pulled toward the earth rots easily, and virtue is destroyed when leaning upon vainglory. A vainglorious monk is a useless worker; he has undergone the toil, but did not receive the reward. A shaken money-bag does not keep what was thrown into it, and vainglory destroys the rewards of virtues. The self-control of a vainglorious man is like the smoke of a furnace, and both shall be dissolved into the air. The wind makes the trace of a man vanish, and so does the almsgiving of a vainglorious man. A stone thrown does not reach heaven, and a prayer of one seeking human approval will not ascend to God.

Chapter 16. Vainglory is a treacherous rock; if you lean upon it, you have lost your load. A wise man hides a treasure, and a prudent monk [hides] the toil of virtue. Vainglory advises praying in the marketplaces, but he who fights this prays into his own treasury. A foolish man publishes his wealth, and moves many to plot against him. But you hide your own things, for on the road you may encounter robbers, until you reach the city of peace and use your things safely. The virtue of a vainglorious man is like a crushed incense burner, and it will certainly not be carried to the altar of God.

Acedia loosens the tension of the soul, but vainglory agitates the mind of one fallen from God; it has made the weak man shout, and the old man stronger than the young, only if many witnesses of the things happening are present; then fasting, wakefulness, and prayer are light, for the praise of the many stirs up the readiness. Do not sell your toils for human glories, nor betray the glory to come through favorable speech. For human glory dwells in dust, and its fame is extinguished upon the earth, but the glory of virtue remains for the age.
Chapter 17. Concerning pride. Pride is a hollow swelling of the soul.

english: Having been filled, if it has become conceited, it will be broken and will cause much sorrow. A flash of lightning foretells the sound of thunder, and pride announces the presence of vainglory.

The soul of a proud man ascends to a great height, and from there it casts him into the abyss. He who has turned himself away from God suffers from pride, and by his own power inscribes his achievements. Just as one who climbs a spider's web and falls through it is driven down, so the one trembling falls by his own power.

Much fruit bends the branches of a tree, and a multitude of virtues humbles the mind of a man. Fruit that has rotted is useless to the farmer, and the virtue of a proud man is of no use to God. A pruning hook carries away a fruitful branch, and the fear of God makes the soul virtuous. Just as the weight of fruit breaks the branch, so pride casts down a virtuous soul.

Do not give your soul to your pride, and you will not see terrible phantasms. For the soul of a proud man is abandoned by God, and becomes a plaything for demons. In the night he fantasizes about a multitude of approaching beasts, and by day he is troubled by thoughts of cowardice; while sleeping he is constantly startled, and while awake he falls under the shadow of an owl. The sound of a leaf startled the proud man, and the sound of water broke his soul. For he who a little ago was opposing himself to God and refusing His help, later is bloodless, under the influence of worthless phantasms.

Pride cast down an archangel from heaven, and made him fall upon the earth like lightning. But humility raises a man to heaven, and prepares him to dance with the angels. Why do you soar, O man, being clay, and rotten in nature, and rising above the clouds? Consider your nature, that you are earth, and ash, and in a little while you will dissolve into dust (Gen 3:19), just now serious, and in a little while...

english: The scorpion. Why do you lift up your neck for that which in a little while will be rotting? A great man helped by God has been abandoned, and the weakness of nature has been recognized. You have nothing that you have not received from God; why then do you plant yourself in another's [property] as if it were your own? Why do you adorn the grace of God as if it were your own possession? Recognize the Giver, and do not lift yourself up too much; you are a creature of God, do not deny the Creator; helped by God, do not deny the Benefactor. You ascended to the height of a position, but He guided you there; you established virtue, but He worked it. Acknowledge the one who exalted you, so that you may remain firm in that height; recognize the one who is of the same kind, because He is of the same essence. Do not deny the kinship through arrogance.

Chapter 19. That person is humble, and proportionate; but the same Creator fashioned both. Do not despise the humble; for he has been established more securely for you; he walks upon the earth, and does not fall quickly; but the lofty one, if he falls, will be shattered. A proud tree is one without roots, and it will not withstand the blow of a wind. A walled city, a blind intellect, and the one dwelling in it will be safe. A wind-blown grain is tossed about, and the blow of a wind lifts up the proud; a cracked vessel will be destroyed, and the memory of the proud is blotted out. The word of the humble is a polishing of the soul, but the word of the proud is filled with arrogance. The prayer of the humble bends God down, but the petition of the proud provokes God. Humility is the roof of a house, and it keeps the one ascending safe. When you ascend to the height of virtues, then you have great need of security. For he who falls from the ground is quickly raised, but he who falls from on high risks death. A precious stone is fitted to a golden setting, and a man's humility is beautified by many virtues.
